title: Lesson 7: Templates That Scale: Parameterized Prompts You Reuse With Different Inputs
description: Parameterized prompts: a fixed frame written once with a few named variable slots filled fresh each run, why the stable frame beats re-deciding the prompt every time, and the judgment about when a task earns a template at all.

questions.question: Nadia wants her weekly client brief to come back the same shape every Monday so her sponsor can scan it in thirty seconds. Per the lesson, what is the single most important thing to write once and keep stable?
options: The fixed frame: the role, audience, tone, output format, and review criteria that never change from week to week
The exact numbers that appeared in last week's brief
A fresh, fully rewritten prompt every Monday so each brief is unique
The name of the chat tool she happens to be using that week
questions.explanation: The lesson argues the value of a template is mostly in the fixed frame, not the fill-in. Nadia's stability comes from a frame (role, audience, tone, format, criteria) written once, so only the four slots change. The other options either vary the frame itself or treat the fresh material, not the stable frame, as the source of consistency.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what is the right way to keep a template's variable slot from being misread as part of the instruction?
options: Mark the variable input as its own clearly labeled slot (a named bracket or divider) so the model treats it as today's data, not a rule
Hide the fresh material entirely so the model has to guess what changed
Write the fresh input in the same tone as the instructions and let the model sort it out
Add as many slots as possible so every detail has its own placeholder
questions.explanation: The lesson cites Anthropic's guidance that structuring a prompt so the variable input is clearly marked reduces the chance the model misreads a slot as part of the instruction. Hiding the input, blending it into the instructions, and adding sprawling slots all contradict the lesson's emphasis on few, well-named slots and clearly separating the variable from the fixed.

questions.question: A colleague asks whether she should build a reusable template for an irregular, judgment-heavy task that happens once or twice a year. Per the lesson, what is the right call?
options: Do not build it; a template only pays off when the task recurs often and the frame stays stable, and a one-off leaves the setup unused
Build it anyway because every task benefits from a fixed format
Build it and force the task to fit the frame, since templates always improve output
Build a separate template for every single variation the task could hit
questions.explanation: The lesson says a template earns its keep only when two things are true: the task recurs often enough that the setup pays for itself, and the frame is genuinely stable across runs. A rare, judgment-heavy, irregular task is exactly the case the lesson flags where a one-off prompt is the better choice. The other options recommend templates where the lesson recommends against them.
